definition: The set of standard fee types that make up what a shipper pays a pipeline to move gas, as itemized in pipeline tariffs.
core_idea: Pipeline transportation cost is built from several distinct charge types — some fixed, some variable, some paid in gas rather than cash — rather than a single price.
key_points: Commodity charge: a variable, per-unit charge for the gas actually transported.
Reservation charge: a fixed monthly fee paid to reserve transportation capacity, independent of how much gas is actually shipped.
Fuel usage: gas physically lost/consumed in transit, commonly taken by the pipeline as in-kind payment to fuel the compressors that move the gas.
GRI charge: a small fixed U.S. pipeline charge that funds the nonprofit Gas Research Institute.
Receipt adder and delivery adder: fixed price adjustments that translate a nearby benchmark price into the price at the specific receipt point or delivery point, respectively.
Postage stamp rate: a single flat transportation charge that applies pipeline-wide on a pipeline with only one rate zone, regardless of actual distance shipped.
relationships: Delivery adder and receipt adder both key off a nearby benchmark price rather than being set independently.
trading_implications: A shipper's all-in transport cost mixes fixed elements (reservation charge, GRI charge) with volumetric ones (commodity charge, fuel usage), so cost per unit shipped falls as utilization rises.
caveats: Fuel usage is not a cash fee — it is gas volume that never arrives, effectively paid in kind.
